newsitem.title: USA: Clinton raising $2 million for Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Clinton raising $2 million for Democrats.

text.p: Two days after appealing anew for campaign finance reform, President Clinton was back on the road Monday tapping donors for another $2 million for the debt-ridden Democratic Party.

Clinton raised the money at a fund-raising lunch in Boston and events planned for Monday night in New York, including a performance of the Broadway play, "A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum," featuring Whoopi Goldberg.

In remarks to 500 people at the lunch, half of whom were invited as thanks for past work and were not asked not to give money, Clinton said he appreciated Boston's support in the year after Republicans took control of Congress in 1994 elections and his own re-election in 1996 looked doubtful.

"Thank you for being here for us in 1995, when everyone said the days of our administration were numbered, the Democratic Party was on a down hill. You know all that stuff they said. You were right, and they were wrong, and I thank you for that," Clinton said to applause in a crowded ballroom at the Copley Plaza Hotel.
He said he wanted to prepare America for the 21st century and "lead the world toward peace, freedom and prosperity and to give our chidollaren a better future than any generation has ever known."
"That's what I'm dedicated to. We've got 3 1/2 more years to work for it, and your presence here today has dramatically increased the chances that we will succeed," he said.

Democratic National Committee officials said the party's debt hanging over from last year's campaigns totalled $14.4 million, but that only 15 cents out of every dollar raised was going to debt reduction, with the rest to organising campaigns, helping candidates and party-building.

The Boston fund-raiser included contributions of $500 to $25,000. In New York, a reception was $1,000 per person, a New York dinner was $5,000 a plate and the Broadway show featured donations of $125 to $25,000. Officials said more than $1 million was being raised in Boston and $1 million in New York.

After the controversy over the way Democrats raised money last year, which has led to a Justice Department investigation and Senate oversight hearings that start next week, Clinton proposed to reform the way campaigns are financed to ban large, unregulated "soft money" contributions.

In the last few months, Clinton has made it a staple of his second term to one day urge Congress to reform campaign financing then the next day urge big-money contributors to dig deep into their pockets for the "soft money" contributions that would be banned under reform.
Just last Saturday, Clinton lamented the fact that Congress would not approve campaign finance reform by the July 4 deadline he had proposed in his State of the Union address in January.
In his radio address Saturday, he said he wanted to end the "ever-escalating arms race," blamed Congress for the failure to achieve reform and urged Americans not to "let them get away with it."
